title: Find Users With Valid E-Mails
statement:
One table lists the accounts of a website:

- `Users(user_id, name, mail)`: one row per account; `user_id` is unique. Some `mail` values are malformed.

A mail address is **valid** when it consists of a prefix immediately followed by `@leetcode.com`, with nothing after it:

- the prefix's first character is a letter (`a`–`z` or `A`–`Z`), so the prefix cannot be empty;
- each later prefix character is a letter of either case, a digit, an underscore `_`, a period `.` or a dash `-`;
- the ending is case-sensitive: only the all-lowercase `@leetcode.com` counts, so `@LeetCode.com` or `@leetcode.COM` makes the address invalid.

Report every user whose mail is valid, with the columns `user_id`, `name` and `mail`. Rows may come in any order.
constraints: Text comparisons and REGEXP ignore case by default, as in MySQL
brute:
SELECT user_id, name, mail
FROM Users
WHERE CHAR_LENGTH(mail) > 13
  AND HEX(RIGHT(mail, 13)) = HEX('@leetcode.com')
  AND LEFT(mail, 1) REGEXP '^[a-zA-Z]$'
  AND LEFT(mail, CHAR_LENGTH(mail) - 13) NOT REGEXP '[^a-zA-Z0-9_.-]'
notes:
## Intuition

Validity is a property of one row's text, so this is a filter: keep the rows whose `mail` matches a pattern. The rule (a letter, then any run of allowed characters, then a fixed lowercase domain, and nothing before or after) is exactly what a **regular expression** anchored at both ends describes. One detail decides the problem: MySQL compares text without case by default, so the match has to be made case-sensitive or `@LEETCODE.COM` would slip through.

## Approach

1. Read every row of `Users` and select `user_id`, `name` and `mail` unchanged.
2. Keep a row when `REGEXP_LIKE(mail, pattern, 'c')` is true. The pattern `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*@leetcode[.]com$` reads:
   - `^[A-Za-z]`: the first character is a letter;
   - `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]*`: zero or more allowed characters (the dash is last in the class so it means itself);
   - `@leetcode[.]com$`: the literal domain, with `[.]` for a real period, ending the string.
3. The match type `'c'` makes the comparison case-sensitive; that is why the letter classes spell out both `A-Z` and `a-z`.

## Example 1, step by step

- `winston@leetcode.com`, `bella-@leetcode.com` and `sally.come@leetcode.com` start with a letter, use only allowed characters and end in the domain: kept (users 1, 3, 4).
- `jonathanisgreat` has no domain; `david69@gmail.com` has the wrong one.
- `quarz#2020@leetcode.com` contains `#`, which no part of the pattern accepts.
- `.shapo@leetcode.com` starts with a period, so `^[A-Za-z]` fails.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · L) for n users and mail length L; the pattern is checked once per row.
- Space: O(n) for the result.

## Pitfalls

- A bare `.` in a pattern matches any character, so `@leetcode.com$` also accepts `@leetcodeXcom` (Test 5); write `[.]` or `\\.`.
- Without `^` and `$` the pattern can match in the middle: `#eve@leetcode.com` and `eve@leetcode.com.au` would pass (Test 6).
- `mail REGEXP ...` and `LIKE '%@leetcode.com'` ignore case in MySQL, so an uppercase domain is wrongly accepted (Test 4).
- The first character must be a letter: digits, `_`, `.` and `-` are allowed only later (Test 3).

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Users` | the only table; every column is reported as stored |
| `REGEXP_LIKE(text, pattern, 'c')` | 1 when `text` matches `pattern` case-sensitively |
| `^`, `$` | anchor the pattern to the whole mail |

narration.1: The three columns are reported exactly as stored.
narration.2: Every user is a candidate; validity depends only on the row's own mail.
narration.3: The anchored pattern demands a leading letter, only allowed characters after it, and the exact domain; the match type c makes it case-sensitive so the domain must be lowercase.
